Moses. The greatest prophet and lawgiver in Hebrew scripture, credited with liberating the Israelites from slavery in Egypt and giving them the Torah at Mount Sinai.

Born to Hebrew slave parents, Moses was placed in a basket on the Nile River by his mother to escape Pharaoh's decree that all Hebrew male infants be killed. He was adopted and raised as an Egyptian prince by Pharaoh's daughter, growing up with royal education and power. At age forty, he killed an Egyptian taskmaster who was beating a Hebrew slave and fled to the wilderness of Midian in fear of discovery.

In Midian, God spoke to him from a burning bush, revealing the divine name YHWH and commanding him to return to Egypt and liberate the Israelites. He led the people through ten plagues of Egypt, each a divine judgment against Egyptian gods and Pharaoh's resistance. The tenth plague, Passover, killed the firstborn of Egypt while sparing Hebrew homes marked with blood on their doorposts.

Moses parted the Red Sea, allowing the Israelites to escape across on dry land while Pharaoh's army pursuing them was swallowed by the returning waters. At Mount Sinai's summit, he received the Ten Commandments written on two stone tablets by the divine finger in the presence of thunder and fire. He then spent forty years wandering with the Israelites in the desert, mediating between God's will and the people's complaints while delivering the laws of the Torah.

He did not enter the Promised Land himself but was permitted to see it from Mount Nebo before his death at age one hundred twenty in perfect health. Jewish tradition holds that he wrote the Torah under divine inspiration, making him not merely a political leader but a scribe of God's word. His role as mediator between God and the people defined the prophetic tradition for all who came after him.
